title: The In-Between Is Still Time: A Small Practice for Waiting
subtitle: A kettle, a queue, a delayed pickup: try leaving one ordinary wait unfilled—not as a test of patience, but as a chance to notice what your mind does when nothing is required of it.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table while a kettle heats; one looks toward the window and the other rests a phone face down beside a mug.
imageConcept: A warm, lived-in kitchen in late afternoon: two friends share a quiet pause at the table while a kettle heats, with one phone resting face down near two mugs and soft window light making the ordinary wait feel spacious rather than staged.
body: Waiting rarely arrives with a label. It slips between the meeting that ended and the ride that is late, between pressing the kettle switch and hearing it click off, between arriving early and being called in. We often treat these intervals as dead air: something to cover with a screen, a task or a little mental rehearsal. That impulse makes sense. A phone offers something to do, and many waits are inconvenient or stressful for good reason. But there is another option for a low-stakes moment: let a minute or two remain open and notice what happens there. Not to become more patient, and not to turn an ordinary pause into a self-improvement assignment. Just to experience a small piece of the day without immediately directing it elsewhere.
A pause is not a performance

The invitation is modest: leave one safe, ordinary wait unfilled if that feels comfortable. You do not need to sit perfectly still, empty your mind or make the moment meaningful. You can notice the kettle’s low hum, the light on the counter, or the fact that your attention has already moved on to what comes next. You might feel restless. You might feel nothing in particular. Either is a real response, not a score. This matters because “be mindful” can sound like one more demand placed on a day already crowded with them. Here, mindfulness means paying some attention to what is happening, including impatience or the wish to check a message, without insisting that either must change. The pause belongs to you; ending it belongs to you, too.

In six experiments, university-student participants expected quiet time to think would be less enjoyable and engaging than they later reported it to be. That finding suggests people may underestimate what an unstructured interval can offer in the study settings; it does not show that everyone will enjoy waiting, or that the same result applies to a tense or consequential delay [1]. A separate study asked 99 people to wait alone in an empty room for 7.5 minutes. Participants who felt more bored also tended to feel that time was passing more slowly and to think about time more often [2]. These are useful observations about particular situations, not proof that a short mindful pause will make time move faster, reduce worry or suit everyone. The practice here is an invitation informed by research, not an intervention tested by those studies.
Why the phone is not the villain

A screen can be useful company. It can help you check a bus, reach someone, read, listen or make a necessary wait easier. There is no universal rule that a phone makes a pause worse. Still, one set of experiments offers a reason to notice how we use it: across seven experiments involving 1,223 participants, switching between or within online videos could increase boredom and reduce satisfaction or engagement. The findings were less conclusive for online articles and for people outside university samples [3]. That is evidence about particular kinds of video switching—not a verdict on every phone, app or person. It may simply help explain why opening one clip, then another, does not always feel like a satisfying way to spend a spare minute. The useful question is not “Should I use my phone?” but “Am I choosing this, or reaching for it automatically?”
Choose the right kind of wait

Start with a moment where your attention is genuinely available. Water heating, a friend finishing a short errand, or sitting in a waiting room before an appointment begins may work. Avoid waits that require vigilance: driving, supervising a child, watching traffic, monitoring something that could become urgent, or staying alert for important information. A low-stakes pause is not the place to ignore a message you need to receive. Nor does every emotionally charged wait need to become a mindfulness exercise. If you are waiting for difficult news, a medical result or someone’s safe arrival, you can choose company, information, movement or support instead. The point is not to prove you can tolerate discomfort. It is to make room for an ordinary interval when that room feels available.
Try a minute without directing it

When a suitable wait appears, begin by naming it plainly: “I’m waiting for the kettle,” or “I’m early for this appointment.” Let your eyes rest on something nearby. Notice one simple detail—the shape of a mug, a patch of sun, the sound of a ventilation fan. Then notice where your mind goes. It may start planning dinner, replaying a conversation, or wondering how long the wait will last. You do not need to follow every thought, argue with it or replace it with a positive one. If the impulse to reach for your phone appears, register it without making it a problem: “I want to check.” Then decide. You can keep waiting, look at the screen, or end the experiment. The choice is the practice; the screen is not a failure.

For some people, quiet space can make thoughts feel louder. A pause may bring up loneliness, anxiety, grief or a worry that is difficult to set aside. There is no virtue in pushing through that. Open your eyes, change what you are attending to, use your phone, talk to someone or move on with the task. If the wait itself involves distressing or high-stakes news, a small attention exercise is not a substitute for support or useful information. You might choose to make the interval less solitary: send a message, ask someone to sit with you, or decide what practical next step would help. The practice is optional precisely because people and circumstances differ. If it is not useful today, that is information about today—not a measure of your patience.
Let the kettle be the whole experiment

The next time water is heating and you have nothing you must monitor, try one minute. Say to yourself, “I’m waiting for the kettle.” Notice one thing in the room, then let your attention wander where it will. You do not have to slow your breathing, reach a conclusion or keep your phone out of reach. If you pick it up, notice that and choose what you want next; if the pause becomes uncomfortable, end it. When the kettle clicks off, the experiment is over. You might have found the minute pleasant, dull, busy or barely noticeable. Let that be enough. The aim is not to make waiting beautiful. It is to discover, once in a while, that a small interval can be lived rather than merely filled.
